summary:
Ekiti State stands within Nigeria's uniform national criminalisation framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at the border. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria, updated by 19 August 2026 and reported by SaharaReporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity; of death-penalty risk under Sharia provisions in some northern states; and of liability for those who help arrange or attend a same-sex wedding. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public.

Enforcement in Ekiti State is documented. Human Rights Watch records that on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened her with 14 years in prison; the report states she was beaten at least twice over the period. In September 2014 a gay man was arrested at the Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and was released after two days in detention after paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend. Also in 2014 a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.

Trans-specific violence is documented nationally. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Detention carries a specific placement risk for trans women. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement across the country. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

A regional-magazine report on queer life in the federal capital documents threats and police raids alongside informal community organising, and community grief after the August 2024 killing of a prominent transgender content creator. The pattern of official indifference after that killing, with no charges six months on, is consistent with the absence of any protection machinery for LGBT+ people in Nigeria.

Ekiti's experience is one data point within a nationwide regime rather than an exception: the same statute, the same penalties and the same policing practices apply in every state, with the additional layer of Sharia criminal law in twelve northern states.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ekiti State have absorbed the SSMPA as an everyday instrument of policing rather than a distant statute. Human Rights Watch records a September 2014 arrest at the Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti that was a gay man's third arrest, indicating repeated round-ups in the same venues, and a 2014 incident in which a state investigator in Ado Ekiti extorted a 25-year-old gay man.

Health services in the state capital are not usable safely by trans residents. Debbie, beaten in Ado Ekiti in January 2014, was unable to access Ekiti health services and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, a journey that recurs as the practical cost of routine care.

Community organising continues informally despite the absence of any legal protection, and residents live alongside the knowledge that gender expression, not only conduct, attracts police attention.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here; the sources establish fear of the proposals, not their status.

No Ekiti State instrument beyond the national SSMPA, and no state-level hate-crime or protection provision, is sourced; whether Ekiti has adopted any complementary legislation is not established.

The placement of trans women between male and female prison sections in Nigeria is left to discretion on the available evidence; the October 2024 panel addressed the security classification of Bobrisky's detention, not a general rule on section assignment.

Whether suspects were ever charged in the August 2024 killing of a transgender woman in Abuja is unresolved beyond the February 2025 finding that no charges had been brought six months after the killing.

The reported extortion and bribe amounts rest on single-source accounts and are not independently corroborated in this inventory.
